summary: Rest day in St. Louis: one rider walked about two hours to the Gateway Arch, the team bought the national park sticker there, and they had dinner with hosts and their friends.
slept_at: Airbnb in St. Louis (host's neighborhood, The Grove)
planning_notes: Gateway Arch (St. Louis) sells the national park sticker for bikes.

summary: Rode 83 miles from St. Louis suburbs onto the Katy Trail and ended at a treehouse in Hermann, MO; the rider ran out of food by mile 35 and arrived late.
slept_at: Treehouse in Hermann, MO (host not named)
planning_notes: First ~20 miles out of St. Louis are suburbs with highway exit ramps and a wrong turn risk; the Katy Trail starts after crossing the Missouri River.
Katy Trail has long stretches with little food; a rider got very hungry by mile 35 with no food stop, so pack extra snacks and lunch.
Hermann MO: ice cream shop and cafe next to each other were a team favorite.

summary: Easy 51-mile Katy Trail ride from Hermann to Jefferson City; the team had bike fit checks at a local shop, cooked Japanese curry for the host, and went to the host's brewery gig.
slept_at: Host Sarah's house, Jefferson City, MO
contacts: Sarah, host in Jefferson City, MO (musician; performed at a local brewery)
Local bike shop in Jefferson City, MO (bike fit checks for two riders; shop not named)
planning_notes: Katy Trail's crushed-stone surface takes more effort than pavement; 50 trail miles felt slower than expected.
Jefferson City: ride up The Skywalk (spiral ramp) to reach the Jefferson City Bridge when entering the city from the trail.
Jefferson City is worth a rest day; the team felt they did not explore it.

summary: Rode 60 miles from Jefferson City to Sedalia, MO in a flat, low-morale slog; the team had a famous barbecue lunch at Kehde's and slept in Antioch church with only a hose for showers.
slept_at: Antioch church, Sedalia, MO (church host)
contacts: Pastor Jeff and his wife Ann, Antioch church, Sedalia, MO (hosts; recommended Kehde's Barbeque)
Sarah and Josh, hosts in Jefferson City, MO (made biscuits and gravy; Sarah sang for them as they left)
planning_notes: Antioch church in Sedalia has plenty of floor space but no shower; the team showered with a garden hose.
Kehde's Barbeque in Sedalia (seating in a train car) is a strong food stop; pulled pork and root beer floats; vegetarians may find it limited.
Mid-trip Missouri days were tedious; the team suggested a rest day in Jefferson City.

summary: First century (118.85 miles) from Sedalia, MO to Osawatomie, KS, taking 13 hours; branches on the Katy Trail damaged derailleurs, and hosts Jeff and Sarah fit bikes and taught maintenance.
slept_at: Hosts Jeff and Sarah's home, Osawatomie, KS
contacts: Jeff and Sarah, Osawatomie, KS (retired doctors; run a bike repair and fit shop from their garage; gave free bike fits and a maintenance crash course)
planning_notes: Riding side by side on the Katy Trail's last stretch meant branches and twigs hit everyone; the team's derailleurs took the damage. Ride staggered on trails with debris.
Sedalia to Osawatomie is 118 miles and took 13 hours with the Katy Trail's 60 miles; a 100+ mile day needs a planned early start and a driver for water and food.
Osawatomie, KS: free bike fits and maintenance advice from the hosts; a good stop before the Flint Hills.

summary: Riders were caught in a severe thunderstorm on the Flint Hills Trail and then KS-68 (no shoulder, heavy semis), took refuge in a cafe, and added a 10-mile gravel detour around a flooded trail to reach Council Grove, KS.
slept_at: Cottage House B&B, Council Grove, KS
contacts: Jeff and Sarah, Osawatomie, KS (hosts; escorted riders to the Flint Hills Trail)
planning_notes: KS-68 out of Osawatomie has no shoulder and heavy semi-truck traffic; one rider pulled over after a close pass. Avoid it or plan a trail route.
Flint Hills Trail turns muddy and slow after rain, and sections flood; a flooded stretch forced a 10-mile gravel detour that was rocky.
The team had no agreed storm plan and spent about 30 minutes in indecision; agree on a storm protocol (when to pull off, where to shelter) before the trip.
Hosts asked every week what the team would do in a storm; have a real answer ready.

summary: Rode 73 miles from Council Grove to Newton, KS into a 20 mph headwind and 110 F heat index, then a lightning storm with 60-70 mph gusts near Walton; three riders took refuge in a ditch and a host van picked them up.
slept_at: Host Janet, Orvin, and John's home, Newton, KS
contacts: Janet, Orvin, and John, hosts in Newton, KS (cooked spaghetti and mulberry pie; Orvin picked up riders after the storm)
John, host in Walton/Newton, KS (drove his van through the storm to pick up riders)
planning_notes: Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve (KS) has a visitor center with a national park sticker and a 2-mile gravel trail; bison visible at a distance.
Kansas Hwy 50 headwinds (about 20 mph) pushed one rider to 8 mph; start early and plan water and shade stops.
Lightning on open Kansas roads with no shelter for miles: a gas station in Walton was the nearest refuge; ask hosts or the driver for shelter options before leaving.
A support van got three riders off the road after a storm; keep the van within calling distance of riders on exposed days.

summary: Ran a learning festival at the Newton Public Library with Tinkercad bubble-wand design and 3D printing, strawberry DNA extraction, and physics demos; the team then had ice cream at Braum's and pizza with their hosts.
slept_at: Hosts Orvin and Janet's home, Newton, KS
learning_festival: Newton Public Library, Newton, KS (4th learning festival): Tinkercad bubble-wand design and 3D printing with a talk on 3D printing applications, strawberry DNA extraction, and physics demos (Physics of Sound).
contacts: Orvin and Janet, hosts in Newton, KS
Newton Public Library (learning festival venue, about a 10-minute walk from the host home)
planning_notes: Students' Tinkercad designs often float or have disconnected pieces; the team had to fix them before printing, so allow prep time.
Print backlog: a batch of bubble wands ran late, and the last class period was given to printing. Start prints early.
One student's castle design would have taken too long to print and had to be shortened; set a print-time limit for designs.
The library's outdoor patio and the nearby host home made logistics easy.

summary: Rode US-50 across the Kansas prairie and celebrated July 4 with hot dogs and sparklers; the planned Stafford RV Park was swapped for a legal stealth camp at the Highway 50 rest area.
slept_at: Highway 50 rest area near Stafford, KS (legal stealth camp; planned Stafford RV Park not used)
planning_notes: A Highway 50 rest area near Stafford, KS allowed legal overnight camping when the RV park plan changed.

summary: Flat 76-mile US-50 ride from Stafford to Dodge City, KS through a 17-mile wind farm; a rider got a first flat that was fixed roadside with a hand pump, and the team visited Paleteria La Michoacana and Boot Hill Museum.
planning_notes: US-50 across Kansas is flat with wide shoulders and few turns; good for steady-pace riding but can have headwinds and thunderstorms.
A 17-mile wind farm on US-50 near Dodge City took more than an hour with wind; expect slow miles there.
Carry a hand pump: a flat on the US-50 shoulder was fixed roadside; a second rider also had a flat that day.
Paleteria La Michoacana in Dodge City is a standout food stop (popsicles and esquites).
Boot Hill Museum's gun show had ended before the team arrived; check show times.

summary: A driving day for the van: the driver helped a rider fix a flat, bought lunch and supplies in Garden City, and had pizza at Victory Baptist Church; the post is mostly a personality quiz.
slept_at: Inn booked by Victory Baptist Church, Lakin, KS
contacts: Pastor Kenton, Victory Baptist Church, KS (dinner and booked the lodging)
planning_notes: The support van can reach a rider with a flat on the road; the driver went to help one rider fix a flat.
Garden City, KS has a Walmart the team used for supply runs (used twice in one day).

summary: Rode 78 miles from Lakin, KS to Lamar, CO through a rain shower and crossed into Colorado; one rider toured a large Kansas dairy farm in the morning, and the team cooked a dinner in a bar's industrial kitchen after sleeping in a motel converted to dorms.
slept_at: Motel converted to dorms by Lamar Community College, Lamar, CO
contacts: Ed, farmer in Lakin, KS (gave a tour of a 32,000-acre dairy with about 5,000 cows)
Lamar Community College, Lamar, CO (hosted the team in converted motel dorms)
Trustee of Lamar Community College who owns a bar (let the team use its industrial kitchen)
planning_notes: Lakin, KS: the dairy farm tour offered by a local farmer is a good rest-day activity.
The Welcome to Colorado sign on US-50 is a photo stop; climbing it gives splinters.
Lunch park just over the Colorado line had heavy fly swarms.
Lamar: a bar's industrial kitchen is a good place to cook for the whole team.

summary: Lamar, CO rest day: the team ran a strawberry DNA learning festival on the library patio, then went to Pike's Tower and a park, and ate Indian food in the motel parking lot.
slept_at: Dorm rooms in Lamar, CO (converted motel by Lamar Community College)
learning_festival: Lamar, CO library patio (5th run of the workshop): strawberry DNA extraction; kids discussed cloning and chose which fruits to test next.
contacts: Lamar Community College, Lamar, CO (dorm housing)
planning_notes: The library patio worked well for an outdoor learning festival: sun, a circle on the pavement, and good plant-genetics discussion.
Pike's Tower in Lamar does not show the Rockies or Pikes Peak because trees block the view.
Indian takeout in Lamar took two hours to pick up; order ahead.
BJ's ice cream in Lamar is a local favorite; order from the phone at the window.

summary: Hot, flat, dry 86-mile ride from Lamar to Fowler, CO with few services; the post is a team packing-list review and a donation request for gear.
planning_notes: Packing: one carry-on plus one backpack per rider; the minivan had limited space for camp gear, learning festival supplies, food, and water.
Items the team did not use: a disc, a Flipper Zero, an umbrella, and a retainer; leave these at home.
A rider was short on gear and asked for donations of bike shorts, socks, sports bras, shoes with soles attached, portable chargers, and pajamas.
Eastern Colorado (Lamar to Fowler) is hot, flat, and dry, with middle-of-nowhere gas stations as the only stops.

summary: Rode 99.76 miles from Fowler to Colorado Springs over desolate, hot terrain; one rider showed early heat stroke symptoms, and the team had dinner with an MIT alum and went to a college rodeo.
contacts: Mark, MIT alum, and his wife Rachel's family, Colorado Springs, CO (dinner; Frito pie and white chicken chili)
planning_notes: The post office about 60 miles into the Fowler to Colorado Springs route had no tables or shade; the next town is about 10 miles further and has a park for lunch.
Heat stroke symptoms (shivers) hit a rider on this stretch; plan shade and water stops in eastern Colorado.
Horseflies were heavy on this route; they bit through sleeves and gloves.
The Colorado Springs rodeo (college rodeo in July) is a good evening event; the team only caught the last 45 minutes.

summary: Rode 61 miles from Colorado Springs to Denver on bike-friendly roads; the rider's father met them on the road, and the host David offered bike safety checks while the rider hunted for brake pads.
slept_at: Hosts Maud and David's home, Denver, CO
contacts: Maud and David, hosts in Denver, CO (David did bike safety checks; invited MIT alumni to dinner)
MIT alumni guests at the Denver dinner (ranging from recent grads to class of 1977; shared career advice)
planning_notes: Colorado Springs to Denver is one of the more bike-friendly stretches: many cyclists and considerate drivers; 14 cyclists were counted before lunch.
Brake pads: three bike shops gave conflicting advice on which pads fit each bike; bring the exact part number or have a mechanic check.
Daniels Park (lunch stop after a 500 ft climb) has prairie dogs; the team learned they can carry plague, so keep away from them.
Hosts offered bike safety checks in Denver, so book those ahead.

summary: Denver rest day: moved from one host's house to another, visited Spokes alum Kate, shopped at REI, toured Red Rocks (closed for a concert), and explored RiNO with a local friend.
slept_at: Host Li Lee's home, Denver, CO
contacts: Li Lee, host in Denver, CO (shared stories about an RV trip across the country)
Maud and David, hosts in Denver, CO (earlier house; breakfast)
Kate, Spokes 2018 alum in Denver, CO (lunch and LoHi recommendations)
planning_notes: Red Rocks Amphitheatre was closed for a concert and the Dino Ridge Trail was too far for a same-day dinner; check the event calendar.
When switching hosts, check every bike and bag: one bike was left at the first house and had to be retrieved.
A LoHi ice cream shop gave free toppings and a size upgrade after the team said they were riding across the country; asking can get free food.
REI in Denver: the bike shorts selection was weak; the team did not buy there.

summary: Tried to ride US-285 out of Denver and then a ten-mile Conifer climb; the 285 was too scary (one rider nearly hit by a truck on a downhill), so five riders shuttled to the Kenosha Campground, CO (the post lists 44.8 miles and 4,196 ft ridden against 74.6 miles and 7,556 ft planned).
slept_at: Kenosha Campground, CO
contacts: Unnamed bike shop in Conifer, CO (straightened the derailleur hanger; this was the third time it was bent)
Unnamed household on the Conifer climb (set out water for cyclists)
planning_notes: US-285 out of Denver: busy, with exit-only lanes to cross and a narrow shoulder on steep downhill curves; trucks passed within inches. The team recommends avoiding it.
The Conifer climb (about 10 miles, High Grade Road section) is steep and hot; a house on the route sets out water for cyclists.
Carry a spare derailleur hanger; this rider's was bent three times on the climbs.
Denver's bike trails are busy and well built, with roundabouts and bike lanes.
Kenosha Campground (CO) has no showers; the team used wipes.

summary: Ride from Kenosha Campground to Buena Vista, CO (65.3 miles): gravel on Elkhorn Road was too loose so the riders turned back, the US-285 descents were terrifying, and after a flat fix and a wait at the CO-9 junction the group kept riding the 285 to Buena Vista.
contacts: Hungry Moose Caboose gas station on US-285 near the campground (lattes, hash browns, breakfast sandwiches)
planning_notes: US-285 steep descent right out of the campground (near -10 percent grade), narrow shoulder, heavy traffic on the curves: avoid.
Elkhorn Road (dirt per Google Street View) was 20 miles of loose gravel and dust; a driver confirmed the rest was the same. Check current conditions with locals, not satellite photos.
The US-285 stretch between Fairplay and the US-24 junction has the widest shoulders on that road.
Fairplay, CO: lunch with Palisade peaches and bowls was a good stop.
A hand pump only reached about 40 psi; for curvy mountain descents, have support bring a floor pump.
Cars graze riders on the last stretch of US-24 into Buena Vista; shuttle that part if the team is not comfortable.

summary: Buena Vista rest day: hiked Harvard Lakes in the Collegiate Range, swam in the cold lake, met Stanford Spokes for dinner in Salida, and returned to find tents blown over in a storm on the host's lawn.
slept_at: Host Dan's lawn, Buena Vista, CO (camping)
contacts: Dan, host in Buena Vista, CO (tent camping on his lawn)
Stanford Spokes team (dinner in Salida, CO; shared advice on US-50 and Utah national parks)
planning_notes: Hike: Three Elk Creek Trailhead to Harvard Lakes (AllTrails has the trail); riders recommend turning back in hail and storms.
Stake tents to the ground on a windy host lawn; the team did not and the tents blew over in a storm.
Salida, CO: a Mexican restaurant was a good spot for a large group dinner.

summary: Rode 68.6 miles from Buena Vista to Gunnison, CO over a 20-mile continuous climb to the Continental Divide, then a fast descent along the Taylor River; hosts Thalia and Jeff cooked dinner.
slept_at: Hosts Thalia and Jeff's home, Gunnison, CO
contacts: Thalia and Jeff, hosts in Gunnison, CO (friends of Maud and David in Denver; League of Women Voters)
planning_notes: Continental Divide from Buena Vista: about 20 miles of continuous uphill with a steep final switchback; a high-grade climb in low gear.
The summit is cold and gusty with snow patches; riders with only desert-weather clothing were under-dressed. Carry a warm layer in the van or on the bike.
Taylor River descent from the Divide to Gunnison is fast (averaged near 30 mph over 5 miles) with hairpins; one rider scraped a knee on a hairpin.
The reservoir lunch stop on the Divide descent is a good break.

summary: Gunnison rest day with a learning festival in town: students made concrete sharks and speakers, and the team had breakfast and a backyard dinner with their hosts Thalia and Jeff.
slept_at: Hosts Thalia and Jeff's home, Gunnison, CO
learning_festival: Gunnison, CO: students made concrete sharks and speakers; one student designed a 3D-printed chicken nugget with a smiley face.
contacts: Thalia and Jeff, hosts in Gunnison, CO (breakfast frittata and garden dinner)
planning_notes: Concrete shark and concrete speaker activities kept kids engaged for the afternoon festival.
Gunnison hosts cook large home meals and welcome the team to their yard; a good rest-day base.

summary: Rode 76.7 miles from Gunnison to Paonia, CO over Kebler Pass (15 miles of gravel downhill) past Crested Butte, and camped in a working orchard among peach trees, picking apricots.
slept_at: Orchard campground on Peach Lane, Paonia, CO
planning_notes: Kebler Pass has about 15 miles of gravel downhill; loose on road bikes, and passing cars kick up dust. The author found that braking on the loose surface caused slides, so a steady line worked better.
Paonia orchard campground: tents sit between peach rows; on July 18 the apricots were ripe, the peaches were not quite.
The orchard store has a cider flight and a rope swing; there is a restaurant on the orchard grounds.
Crested Butte downtown has overpriced coffee and croissants; short stop.

summary: Rode 68.8 miles from Paonia to Grand Junction, CO on a day that was uneventful; the post describes the team's food: bagels, Clif bars, a Wendy's stop in Delta, a salami sandwich lunch, gelato, and a shared dinner.
planning_notes: Riders burned 4,000+ calories per ride by the bike computer's count; pack and buy enough food for big days.
Clif bars can be opened with both hands while the forearms stay on the bars, then eaten one-handed.
Delta, CO: Wendy's at about mile 30 is a quick stop.
Lunch options were thin on this stretch; the team ate on the ground beside a building for shade.

summary: Rode 106 miles (the post lists 106/127) from Grand Junction, CO to Moab, UT along the Colorado River canyons; the border was marked by gravel, three riders had flats within 15 minutes, and one rider had heat exhaustion in the last 10 miles.
slept_at: Camped on the ground in Moab, UT (site not named)
contacts: JJ's Mercantile on UT-128 (sweet tea that helped a rider recover from heat exhaustion)
planning_notes: Grand Junction to Fruita is a paved Colorado River bike path, the best bike path of the trip; Fruita is very bike-friendly for a coffee stop.
Sand-dune road from Fruita into Utah turns from pavement to gravel at the state line; expect flats (three riders had them within 15 minutes).
UT-128 canyons along the Colorado River are very scenic; the last 10 miles into Moab are hot, so stop at JJ's Mercantile for cold drinks.
Cisco, UT is a ghost town with a half-buried car and alien statues; the van waited there.
